claims.text: An ML interatomic potential trained on a reduced ab initio dataset and combined with enhanced sampling can accurately evaluate fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties in multicomponent systems.
Vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling are crucial free-energy contributions near fusion in refractory high-entropy alloys.
A strategically selected set of ab initio configurations can capture the key anharmonic physics needed by the ML potential.
A strategically selected set of ab initio configurations can capture electron–vibration physics in a form reproducible by an ML interatomic potential.
Enhanced sampling can efficiently compute free energies across the solid–liquid phase transition.
The proposed method is applicable near melting and at high temperatures in elemental, binary, and multicomponent alloys.
Local lattice distortions and anharmonic vibrational modes can be encoded in the ab initio training data.
The ML potential can generalize the encoded local distortions and anharmonic modes to reproduce both short- and long-range interactions.
Training on a limited dataset spanning solid and liquid configurations can faithfully reproduce the relevant energy landscape.
The learned energy landscape can retain anharmonic contributions.
The learned energy landscape can retain electron–vibration contributions.
Enhanced sampling will efficiently traverse the free-energy barriers relevant to the phase transition.
The proposed approach will reduce computational cost by at least one order of magnitude relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed approach will reduce computational cost by at least one order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD.
Predicted phase free energies will agree with explicit ab initio results within a 5–10% margin.
Predicted melting temperatures and fusion enthalpies will agree with explicit ab initio results within a 5–10% margin.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations become prohibitively costly for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
TOR-TILD becomes prohibitively costly for complex multicomponent compositions.
The validity of the method depends on obtaining sufficient training data to represent the relevant many-body interactions and configurations.
Poor representation of configurations or dynamical behaviors in the training set can limit the method.
